div.head: NOISY EXHAUST.
div.p: A NOISY EXHAUST.

There are few things I object to more strongly than a noisy exhaust. To me it makes motor cycling a pain rather than a pleasure. And I think it is a point which appeals to all considerate drivers, and I like to class myself among these. Some motor cyclists who would never think of using a "cut-out" have such noisy exhausts that the advantage lies with the "cut-out," since this is only occasionally used, whereas a noisy exhaust is continuous. Every- thing rally depends upon the silencer. If the material of which the pipe is made is light, the escaping gases may strike the pipe with sufficient force to make a considerable noise; in fact, it has the same effect as though it had been struck with a hard substance. It is well worth while to have a good silencer, because such never requires renewing, remain- ing perfect until the machine ultimately finds its way to the scrap heap. A sharp bend in the pipe also makes for noise. The fewer bends there are the more silent is the running.

div.head: HOW TO REVERSE.
div.p: HOW TO REVERSE.

It is curious how many even apparently good drivers bungle when they are called upon to reverse. Personally, I attach a great deal of , importance to it, and when I have been teach- ing anyone to drivel have always taught him how to reverse during the early stages of his initiation. The best way to reverse, I have have always found, is to turn half round in the seat towards the offside, and to hold the top of. the steering wheel with the left hand, while one foot should be on the clutch, and the ether on the foot brake. See that the road is clear, let the clutch in gently, and move elowly backwards. Keep in mind that you must steer in the opposite direction to that of the forward drive, and never give a sudden jerk to correct a swerve. If the car is moving too much to the side, better slip out the clutch and apply the foot brake, bringing the ear to a standstill, and starting afresh.

THE NORTH OF IRELAND.
(Quiwies and correspondence should be addressed to the Editor, c/o "Spokes." Replies can- not be sent by post, and all queries will be glowered in our columns.)

The North of Ireland has been greatly neglected by the cyclist and the motorist, in I spite of the fact that there are few finer d.s- tricts in the United Kingdom. The rugged grandeur of the Donegal shore is unequalled; the scenery is of the wildest character, while ' the whole district is filled with legends and historical associations. Make , Londonderry the starting and finishing points, and proceed by the following route :—Carrigans, 6; Raphoe, IG*; Stranorlar, 9; Barnesmore Gap, 91; Donegal, 81; Killybegs, 171; Carrick, 101; Glen- columbkille, 61; Ardara, 15; Glenties, 51; Dunglow, 131; Falcarragh, Dunfanaghy, 7; Glen, 111; Carrickart, 31; Milford, 91; Rath- mullan, 8; Ferry to Fahan, 21; Londonderry, 91; total 186 miles. Raphoe, a charming spot situated at the foot of the Donegal Mountains, was, until 1835, the seat of a bishopric, and it is commonly supposed that Saint Columba founded a monastery here. The run along the side of Lough Mourne is very fine; then follows thn elimb and descent of the wild Barnesmore Gap, a narrow pass, about five miles long, with the mountains of Barnesmore on the one side and Crough Conellagh on the other, particu- larly trying with the wind against one. Then begins a ride through some of the finest coast scenery imaginable, the country being of the wildest description. The run from Carrick to Ardara is 'through the lovely Glen of St: Columba (Glencolumbkille), one of the most romantic spots in Ireland. The relics of the Saint, including his house and bed, are in the village, which is still a favourite point of pilgrimage. As a matter of fact, the whole I run by the coast from Donegal to Londonderry ' is full of historic interest, which makes it one of the most attractive of all Irish tours. At Rathmullan you take the ferry for Fahan, which lies on the other side of Lough Swilly. Rathmullan is a pretty village, and adjoining it are the ruins of Carmelite Priory, founded in the fifteenth century_ A short run from Fahan, near which is Burt Castle, the home of the M'Devitts, brings one back to London- derry.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 25, 1916.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 25, 1916.
JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
'erence in Horses.
The "Farm and Garden" paragraph respect- ing the sulking habit in horses reminded me of a period when I went out once a week to " do " the district for a weekly paper. One of the

places I had to visit lay in a hollow, and I generally returned on the top of a 'bus run by • a local hotel keeper. It was a slow and toil- some journey, and I took care to make for a seat by the driver whenever there was a vacancy. Observing that he reserved the whip almost ex elusively for one particular horse, I once put in a plea for the poor beast, upon which he explained ,that it was a lazy brute, and would leave the others to do all the work if he did not apply the stimulus directly he noticed any sign of lapse toward the inevitable tendency; thus, in justice to the willing ones, he was obliged tO discriminate.

Well Nursed. , The outside of that 'bus afforded plenty of opportunity for the student of character. Once among my fellow-passengers were a nervous old lady and her husband—that is the proper order, for it was plain that the grey mare was the better horse. The old man had a rear seat, and his wife had somehow imbibed the notion that he might tumble off._ He spoke very quietly, as if ashamed of his partner's extreme solicitude, and we were treated to this sort of thing throughout the journey if p the steep " Are you all right there, Sam?" , "Yes, yes; I'm right enough." "You'll mind and not fall off, won't you?" "I shall not fall off; not I." "Well-, stick fast hold, then." . "Den't worry; there's no danger." "Eh! Just hear that. You're always so reckless, it makes me anxious. (Extra jerk owing to rut in road.) There now; what did I tell you?" "What's up now?" "Why, you nearly fell off, didn't-you? I wish you would take more care of yourself. Eh ! dear me! I shall be glad when we're at th' far end. Now then, now then; there you go again." And sqk forth and so on. It was all very ridiculous and amusing.

Humogen. I confess I was greatly surprised by last week's paragraph demonstrating the iheffective- ness of bacterised peat. Frankly, it was a dis- appointing revelation. From the days when with characteristic whole-heartedness, the late Mr. W. T. Stead boomed the discovery or in- vention in his "Review of Reviews," I have watched developments with considerable interest and increasing confidence. Only two or three weeks ago I spent a couple of hours or so in Professor Rottomley's company, and his enthusi- asm and assurance remained unabated. More- over, his claim was backed by lots of evidence in the shape of successful experiments with his bacterised peat. I am puzzled by last week's contrary assertions. Ambulance Handicap.

The plea for a motor ambulance, and the cow- plaints as to painful delays in horsing the pre- sent one, reminded me of a district in which I once lived, where the splendidly-equipped fire brigade was brought to a high state of efficiency, but was strangely risked for the sake of the pro- verbial " penn'oth of tar." The authorities had an arrangement with the local carriage company to horse the fire engine on occasion, but the company's manager would not bind himself to have horses constantly at hand, so that it hap- pened not infrequently when an alarm was raised that the fire fighters were seriously delayed and hampered. Yet the controlling committee persisted long in this false economy.

" Needless." The appearance of this word at the head of Mr. J. Richardson's letter brought to my mind an experience which no doubt may be paralleled. About half-a-century ago the Corporation of Halifax opened a new road to which they gave the name North-parade. 'Old inhabitants, how- ever, were so convinced that it was a piece of unwarrantable extravagance that they called it "Needless," and so it remained for that genera- tion at least. North-parade is now right in. the heart of a busy industrial district, and a thickly- populated area extends miles beyond. It is an old, old story.

Vegetarian Diet. The one narrated in last week's "thsSsip" is also a fairly common experience. I, too, know those vegetarian banquets. I've had some, an it please you. Moreover, once in Bradford and again in London, I patronised restaurants of the cult, with the like results. In each case I had a reliable guide,, and followed his advice. In both instances the fare.vras "filling," but I soon had to "tighten my belt" and go in search of a "gradely " meal

Distinguished "Old Boy." The honour gained by Midshipman All& pleasantly reflected as it was on Warrington Grammar School, brought to my mind a recent remarkable encounter while taking my walks abroad. Drawing near a Council School, the children of which were in the playground, I spoke to the headmaster, and my greeting led to an interesting conversation. First he showed me a big war map which he had drawn on the gable end of the. building, the respective belligerent cbuntries having distinctive colours —one that is, for Britain and her Allies, and one for Germany and her wretched tools. Then he had me into the assembly room, where were photographs of no fewer than 200 "old boys" who had joined the Colours as eager volunteers long before there was any talk of conscription. A few had made the supreme sabrifice; one had just been recommended for the D.C.M., another had had conferred upon him the greatly-cov,eted Russian Cross of St. George; and most of them wfote to the old teacher in terms of gratitude and affection. The master had a book in which he was careful to paste all newspaper references to any of his boys. He was just organising a scheme for sending suitable parcels of comforts to those of them who were on active service, those who were in hospital, and those who were on home stations, the contents being varied according to circumstances. " Irish lloquence."

Under this heading a few Irish bulls were reproduced last week. Of course, Sir Boyle Roche figured. He it was—as I recollect read- ing a great many years ago—who on one occasion exclaimed "I smell- a rat; I see it floating in the air; but I'll nip it in the bud V" A modern Irish M.P., speaking of suicide, said, "The only way to stop it is to make it a capital offence, punishable with death." Another complained that "As long as Ireland was silent under her wrongs, England was deaf to her cries:" During a debate on the jury question one exclaimed, "By trial by jury have I lived, and, by the blessing of God, with trial by jury I will die." Some English Examples.

It were an error to suppose that such amusing slips were peculiar to natives of the Green Isle, whose emblem many of us were delighted to wear last week-end in honour of the gallantry of her troops. It was an English M.P. who per- petrated the now classic, "You may depend upon it, sir, the pale face of the British soldier is "the backbone of the Indian Army." During a debate on the Army Estimates, one alluded to 1 an item of 11,000,000 as "a fileabite in the ' ocean." When President.of the Board of Trade, Mr. John Burns said on a, memorable occasion, "I should like to throw the honourable member 'a lifeline, so that I might pluck him as a brand from the burning"; and Sir William Hart-Dyke caused much laughter by remarking, "The right honourable gentleman has caught big fish in his time. He has gone to the top of the tree to find them." Another exclaimed "The time has come and is rapidly arriving," and yet another wished a motion was "at the bottom of the 'bottomless pit." Well, did not Milton write "beneath the lowest deep a lower deep."? or something to that effect; my "Paradise Lost" is (a-hem!) misplaced for the moment, so that I quote from memory, though I feel sure I am not far out. ITo proceed—to hasten to a con- clusion, indeed—there is that other classic example of Parliamentary eloquence:—" Why should we beggar ourselves to better posterity? What has posterity done for us?" The laughter ' surprised the speaker, as he was unconscious of his blunder, and he hastened to 'explain": "Sir, by posterity I do not mean our ancestors, but those who come immediately after them."

FARM AND GARDLti.
No Shirking Or Pessimism All WOMEN IN CHESHIRE AGRICUL- Determined And Confident. TURE.

Mr. A. Seymour-Jones, of Wrexham, the father of the late Lieutenant Seymour-Jones, one of the Warrington Territorial officers who have died for their country, recently went to the Front in France, and has been giving some striking impressions of his visit to a Press representative. Mr. Jones, who has been the chief recruiting officer for North Wales, has two other sons, both of whom are serving and are for the moment invalided home from the Front. From these impressions we make the following selections : " I entered into conversation wlth several gunners, who expressed themselves as delighted with the ammunition being sent them, and gave full credit to Mr. Lloyd George. The previous delay in the supply of munitions owing to ,strikes was discussed* and one gunner pertinently summed up the situation in these words: 'You tell those at home to work hard. We will strike here. Let them leave all the striking to us: "The most memorable event we participated in was a review of the Welsh Army under General Owen Phillips by Mr. Lloyd George and 'ourselves, within two miles of the trenches. Amid the roar of the cannon and the " rip " of the machine guns these brave chaps, just out of the trenches, marched past to the martial strains of 'The Men of Harlech,' played by a rass band. Small wonder is it that the sight, and the whole surroundings caused a lump to rise in our throats.

div.head: Lord Newton's Warning And Advire.
div.p: Lord Newton's Warning And Advire.

A meeting of the Cheshire County Committee, which works in connection with the Board of Trade Labour Exchanges, to promote the em- ployment of women in agriculture during the war, was held at Crewe on Monday; The Chairman (Lord Newton) made a state- ment of the work done by the committee in con- nection with the village registration scheme He reported that 160 registrars had been appointed in the county, and that over 400 'village women had registered for agricultural work. Since the formation of the committee it Juno last it was estimated that nearly 500 agri- cultural and horticultural vacancies had been filled. His Lordship said that personally he was not satisfied with these figures, although he under- stood that they compared very favourably with other counties. It was generally agreed that women's labour, where it had been tried, had proved of considerable use, and as far as his limited experience went, it was entirely satis- factory. • 'Lord Newton attributed the general reluctance on the part of,.farmers to /Avail themselves *of the services of women to the deeply-rooted objec- tion in this country to look ahead. In all prob ability more men would be withdrEywn from agriculture, and it was evident that in common with other industries, its interests must also be guarded. He urged the employment of women as the remedy. Several of the district representatives reported their experiences in connection with the village registration scheme in their area. More than 20 meetings have already been held in different parts of the county, with the result that the patriotism of the women has undoubtedly been roused, and that there are now many willing to offer their services to local farmers. It is hoped that the farmers will respond in a similar way, and will -undertake to employ women rather than be -shorthanded. Owing to the enthusiastic response of the women the cora- -1 mittee is in urgent need of more offers of train- ing, and hopes that the farmers will volunteer to train women on their farm,. The lion. The farming situation is becoming serious says "The Times." By this time field work should have been in full swing and a large proportion of the barley and oats already drilled. A promising start was made at the end of January, but for five or six weeks past there has been no progress whatever. The protracted suspension of tillage and seeding operations can scarcely fail to have an adverse effect on the harvest: The oat is the chief cereal affected, and for- tunitely as good crops of this have been grown from seed sown after as,before Lady Day. While the sowing of corn is the first and most urgent operation, the planting of potatoes and the seeding of other vegetables will be due shortly, and is already seasonable. The potato, however, has become a much more accommo- dating crop since the practice of sprouting the tubers before planting has been adopted. This plan is not universal, but it deserves to be.

A great deal can be done in growing potatoes in gardens, allotments, and other small areas. As far as practicable individual householders should endeavour to grow their own require- ments of this and other vegetables, not only as a safeguard against scarcity, but to simplify the task of distribution at a time when the rail- ways may be otherwise fully employed.

"Many of the men were simply delighted at seeing civilians once again. The cheeriest optimism seemed to pervade the whole battle- line, and all the men I spoke to were absolutely confident of victory, but concluded with the in- evitable remark 'But when are the others corn ing r The boys are showing that dogged deter- mination which can only lead to success; they are doing their work as if they are at play, taking their wounds with smiles and giving back more than they get. We saw miles of horses and guns wending their way to the scene of operations, hundreds of motor trans- ports containing 4mmultition, food and other supplies, motor 'buses conveying men to and from the billets and the trenches, and impro- vised railways running from the main roads to the trench reserves; and all these things were going on like clockwork, without a hitch of any kind. .

"Another thilik which impressed us very much was that although we had the pleasure of seeing almost everyone in high command, from Sir Douglas Haigh downward, we never saw a single man who, could be characterised as a 'dug-out,' or as being old, and our experiences brought up ir- resistibly to the conclusion that this is essentially a young man's "war. It should also be 'realised that it is, not;.as is generally understood to be, a military wall. What I mean is this. In the British Army in France to-day there can scarcely be moil!, than a hundred thousand men who are military men by their life's training; on the contrary there are well over a million men who in private life follow commercial pur- suits. One colonel told me that in private life he • was the water engineer of a large city in England, and another that he was a cotton broker, in fact, the men holding the positions of generals of divisions and brigades, colonels, anl so forth are in business and commercial undertakings when at home, and it is this com- mercial and business capacity, plus the modern military trained mind, which is at work in France to-day, and which will eventually beat the Germans. The finest brains of the Empire are at present engaged on this gigantic task, and everything in France is being magnificently organised, and at the same time carried through 'with s'aiot economy. It is not until one 'returns to ngland that one runs up against pessimism, extravagance and muddle. The im- pression created in the mind of our party was that if the spirit which permeates the whole atmosphere at the Froint could only be trans- ferred to England. the period of the war would be very considerably shortened."

div.head: STUPIDITY OF OVERCROWDING.
div.p: THE STUPIDITY OF OVERCROWDING.

A very common fault even 'among otherwise progressive .poultry keepers is that they over- crowd the sleeping quarters. Overcrowding the land is bad enough; to overcrowd the sleeping quarters is even worse. When fowls are kept' too thickly in a house it is impossible to keep them thoroughly healthy, and there is every likelihood of disease breaking out. It stands to reason that if the birds are forced to breathe al bad, vitiated atmosphere the whole night through,it is impossible for them to remain in good health. As a general rule, an adult fowl requires about two square feet of floor space, while ducks should have not less than four square feet, and geese and turkeys six. The height of the house should not be less than six feet at the lowest part, and a poultry house into which a person cannot enter is never to be recommended.

div.head: WHY FOWLS ARE UNHEALTHY.
div.p: WHY FOWLS ARE UNHEALTHY.

Tainted soil, want of green food, and the ex- cessive use of maize are among the most com- mon causes of ill-health. Tainted soil and the excessive use of maize cause liver disease, while lack of green food causes skin and comb trouble —white comb being the most prevalent. While these are the chief dangers to avoid, it does not necessarily follow that fowls kept in close con; finement cannot escape them. One has only to visit some of the crowded industrial centres to , see how these evils are overcome. In some cases gravel or ashes are laid thickly down in thb runs, well beaten or rolled, making a: firm,sur- face, this being frequently removed before any impurity can penetrate below the top coating. Others, who are fortunate enou'gh to have suf- ficient space, halve the run, and use each alternately, thus preventing sour ground.

The chicks will require great care in the mat- ter of overcrowding prevention.. Make a round after dark and see thet none of the houses are overcrowded; remember that as the chicks grow they require more room. Draft any birds which may stand out in size; keep the flocks as uniform as possible. Dry sheds will prove & great advantage during the wet weather we are experiencing; a small dry run should be erected for all chickens, any- thing, which will provide shelter may be arranged, • but take great care that it cannot be easily blown down, or a number of crushed chickens may result. • Make a note of the places in the runs where water gathers; in more suitable weather these should be filled in. Where cinder runs are in use, the run should be carefully swept up every week. Cabbage - stalks and like matter, if left lying about, will quickly become putrid, and should the birds eat such matter, as they will, the result could but be injurious.—" The Poultry World."

div.head: FOUR MEALS A DAY.
div.p: FOUR MEALS A DAY.

The principle of giving four meals, or even more, in the day may not appeal to those who can only attend to their fowls in the morning and evening, but, says "Farm and Homes" it possesses so many advantages that we recom- mend its adoption by all who keep laying hens in small runs entirely for egg-productiofl and are prepared to take reasonable care in feeding. If the latter proviso were not observed the four meals a day would be very disastrous, for the principle consists of giving four 'or more small meals per diem instead of two or three larger ones, and the reason is that, although the birds may not actually, get any more food in the days they have more encouragement to take exercise. For instance, supposing we feed our fowls twice a day. We throw down some corn at each meal, which will keep the hens scratching for an hour or two, or so long as there is anything to be found. Then they will stop, and, with the exception, perhaps, of, an occasional desultory

scratch to see if anything remains, the rest et the day will be passed in comparative idleness, which means that the birds become chilled in winter and become fat and inactive at all times- Then let us try the plan of feeding four times 'a day, and note the difference. We give propor- tionately less, of course, at each meal, but pro- vide something for the birds to scratch for, the effect of which lasts very nearly until the next meal comes round, when they will again beset scratohing. The net result is that the fowls have four of five hours' more exercise during the day, and little if any more food. To carry 011 t this principle it is necessary to combine soft food and hard corn, which is, perhaps, the best plank in other respects for fowls kept in confinement. The soft food is stimulating, and if little is given at first a few grains of bard corn may be thrown down among the Jitter to complete the meal and to provide an incentive for scratching exercised

div.head: MR. GEORGE WALKER . AND SCHOOL EXEMPTIONS.
div.p: MR. GEORGE WALKER . AND SCHOOL EXEMPTIONS.

Sr,—With your permission I should like to deal with one or two statements made by Mr. Walker, the representative of the Working Men's Infirmary Committee, on the Education Committee, at the annual meeting of the former body.

Mr. Walker is reported as saying that the "exemptions averaged about 800 a year, out of 14,000 children." Put in this way, the number of children exempted, to the total number of chil- dren appears small, but the ages of the '14,000 children range from five years to 14 years. Mr. Walker, as a member of the School Attend- ance Committee, should know that no child below the age of 13-years can he exempted from attendance at school, and if he wished to show the proper position, he 'should have given the number of children who were entitled to make• application for exemption, and not the total number of children in the schools. When this comparison is made it will be seen that the teachers are justified in their claim that exemp- tions are granted too liberally by the School Attendance Committee. The last census returns gave the number of children 13 years of age as 1,529. And this may be taken as an approximate number of children who would be entitled by age to make applica- tion for exemption last year, and Mr. Walker tells us that the average number is 800 per annum, i.e., 800 exempted out of 1,500, and not 800 out of 14,000. In other words 50 per cent. of the children are exempted each year. Mr. Walker says the committee kept in view the amount per head necessary to sustain a family, and if the earnings, however small, were necessary to assist in the feeding of the family, they allowed the child tb go to work. Apparently, the reason for the exemption of 800 children is because there is insufficient income in the homes of each of these children properly to sustain the families, or in other words, in 800 Warrington homes la,st year the income was so low that the children bad to be driven to work to help to maintain the family. This is difficult to believe, and if it is true the Working Men's Infirmary Committee would have been better employed in investigating the wages of the fathers of these children, and endeavouring to see what could be done to get them paid a living wage, rather than the children be prematurely put to work in order to subsidise low wages. Mr. Walker says that more than half of the SOO children have passed the VII. or ex-VII. standard. From my own experience ..I am pre- pared to challenge this statement. To quote Mr. Walker, "Statements are more easily made than proved," and it is to be hoped that he 'will exercise a little more restraint when next he sets up to defend the School Attendance Committee, and be a little more sure of his facts. POOR CHILDREN'S FRIEND.
Councillor Skelland Attains His Eightieth Birthday.
STILL "HOLDING THE
FORT."

Councillor James Skelland, of 63, BeWsey- street, and superintendent of the Warrington Ragged School Mission, was eighty years of age last Saturday, when he received the following sympathetic letter from Sir John Kirk, director of the Shaftesbury Society and Ragged School Union :

"Dear Mr. Skelland,—l ,write to join with your many friends in warmcst, congratulations on your birthday. You have a fine record of persistent service for the Master among His little ones. You will long live in the hearts and lives of those to whom you have ministered the Bread of Life; and thus to live on is not to die. I am pleased to know that amid all the dis- couragements of these sad times you are still holding the fort.' May God bless you and pro- long your useful life. In the name of my Council r am sending a little souvenir of our regard for you and for your life-long services." The souvenir was a handsomely bound Bible with a hundred coloured plates, reproduced from the 'original water colour drawings by Harold Copping. In this book were the follow- ing words:—
"To Mr. James Skelland, on his eightieth birthday. A simple recognition of twenty- nine years of devoted service for the poor chil-

dren df the Warrington Ragged School, form- ing part of 75 years' active association with Sunday schbols as scholar, teacher and superintendent. With fraternal neetings and hearty good wishes, of the Coußell of the Sbasiesbury Society and Ragged School Un4on Of LOT don.—John Kirk, director; Arthur Black, hon. secretary."

div.head: SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS OF SUNDAY SCHOOL WORK.
div.p: SEVENTY-FIVE YEARS OF SUNDAY SCHOOL WORK.

As the record in the presentation sets forth, Councillor Skelland has been engaged in Sunday school work in one capacity or another for seventy-five years. From the age of five he was scholar or teacher for 26 years and superin- tendent 20 years; and he has been superin- tendent of the Ragged School (of which he was founder) for the last 29 years. He was born at Hall Green, near Mow Cop, on the 18th March, 1836, his father being a shoemaker. • Times were bad and the family migrated to Hanley, where the mob paraded the streets demanding bread and work. Subsequently his father got work at a stone pit at 2s. a day, with twelve hours to the day. He had no schooling in the accepted sense, because he went to work at the age of seven, and his education he owed almost entirely to Sunday schools. His ea,rly occupa- tions included "gleaning" corn, reaping, carrying bricks at the construction of the rail- way from Congleton to Harecastle, and iron- working at Kidsgrove.

div.head: Roller At Dallarn.
div.p: A Roller At Dallarn.

In 1856, sixty years ago, he became a roller at Dallam Forge, Warrington, which at that time belonged to Messrs. Neil and Company, the chief engineer being Mr. E. Beck. There were fields where Bewsey Forge now stands. Having worked at Dallam continuously for 37 years, with a break of two years when suffering from the results of an accident, he left at the time of the great coal strike. It was in 1877, twenty-nine years ago, that he founded the Warrington Ragged School ' Mission, having resigned the position of super- intendent of the Sunday school at Dallam-lane Chapel to undertake the work among the " ragged " children, for whom nobody appeared to care. He acquired the old school in Dallam- lane on the removal of the congregation to Buckley-street, but there was no furniture, and the neeessacY funds were not forthcoming. A daughter offered him the contents of her money- box as a start and, although the amount was but 3s. 6d., the practical act of sympathy en- couraged him to proceed. He was liberally helped by three friends, Mr. Smethurst and the late Mr.. R. A. Naylor, and the late Mr. Joseph Mounfleld. The First Sunday At The Ragged School. " On the first Sunday in January, 1887," says Councillor Skelland, "the first Ragged School in Warrington was opened. I was assisted by Mr. Robert Dale and my daughter, and in the afternoon, when the other schools had opened, we went out towards Town's End to gather to- gether some of the poorest boys and girls. About a hundred responded to our invitation to come to the Ragged School, and a pathetic sight they presented, for many were completely desti- tute of the comforts of life. They crouched round the stove and some fell asleep under the influence of the heat. We sang a hymn and talked kindly to them. The school has been undenominational from the first, and I hope it will remain so." When the old County. Court in Bank-street was no longer required by the ,Government the premises were secured by the late Mr. Robert Garnett, one of the vice-presidents of the school, for £BB5, and the building was altered for the purposes of the school at a total cost of -21,450, all of which has long since been paid. In 1904 the teachers and workers at the Mission presented Mr. Skelland with photo- g- phic groups of themselves and thp childr , and an Mimi-n.44-.1, a (address. 'which stated :• "Many a young man, and woman at the pre- sent day rejoice for the teaching and guidance you have given them in their early years, and thank God that they were lifted from their miserable home conditions by the influence they received at the Ragged School." The coming of the war greatly interfered with the work of 'the Mission—workers becoming scarce and the boys' band being unable to go out as they have done for years to collect funds for the upkeep of the institution. "But," said Councillor Skelland to' our repre- sentative on Wednesday, "things are adjusting themselves, and we shall be alright, as usual." "How many boys and girls have you had through your hands at tile Ragged School?" we asked. "I really could not tell you," said the Coun- cillor. Councillor Skelland's wife died five years ago last June. .He had a family of one son and three daughters. The boy died young. One daughter i unmarried. Of the other two, one is the/wife of Councillor Rose, chemist, Jarrow, and the other is the wife of Mr. Hayward, iron- monger; Wigan. His sister married Mr. Henry Osborne, late .of St. Barnabas'-place, Lovely- lane, who has recently removed to Congleton. Councillor Skelland is therefore uncle to ex- Councillor E. Osborne.

By MARJORIE.

Patriotic Fasting. The season of Lent has been from time im- memorial associated with fasting, . which this year is as much a patriotic as a pious observ- ance. The National Organising -,Committee /or War Saiings has issued a series of a Done's" that deserve the consideration of both old and young of every class, and medical men have for along time insisted that as a nation we impaired our health and vitality, and shortened our lives by over-eating. Healt:hy adults of ordinary occupation do not require more than eight ounces of butcher's meat per day, and if no consumer ate more than this quantity it would cut down the national butcher's bill by one- third. Such. is the enormous quantity of meat that is not only wasted, but its preparation causes unnecessary household labour, and the ultimate result is to provide work for the doctors. Mr. Edison, the famous American in- ventor, lives on a limited daily ration of solid and liquid food, a custom his family has fol- lowed with the happiest results for several generations.

Servants and War Mirk. Housework will have to be considered from an entirely new and more sensible point of view after the war. It is obviously unpatriotic for a family to employ men servants, who could fight for their country, and such is the demand for women's labour in the munition factories, and on war work, that the retention of female domestics who could be dispensed with, is also denounced as a crime against the community. The result of this cutting down of establish- ments will be that households must be run on more methodical and systematic lines. The lighter duties of a house, and the small details that take up so much time, may not be interest- ing, but they have the advantage of being healthy, and to a great extent housework will cease to, be considered menial and derogatory.

Evening Dresses. • The demand for evening gowns cannot be as limited as is asserted, judging at least from the numbers on view in high-class showrooms. Elderly women have this year more reason than for some time past to complain that designers leave them out of their calculations as far as evening dress is 6oncerned, and bestow their attentions on the youthful only. Gathers, pannier draperies, unlimited yards of frills, and short skirts, ill-become the middle-aged,

although either or all of these are quite fascinating when worn by the slender and youth- ful. The full, short skirt, however, may be worn by those women who are no longer in their first youth,. provided they have retained a slim contour, and there is no disputing the fact that its graceful swing gives an effect of pliancy and slenderness to the figure. • For the young no more becoming style was 'ever invented than the evening skirt, composed of a number of frills of lace or embroidery, or some filmy material, each Of which is stiffened at the edges sufficiently to stand away from—the foundation, to which it is attached. Such a skirt usually has a bodice of some quite sub- stantial material, brocade, satin, or even velvet being used.

The Tight-fitting Bodice. Girls and women who possess good figures are now given an advantage denied them during the sloppy period of the blouse and bodice. The demure, almost tight-fitting corsage, gains in importance every day, and is certain of a vogue as spring advances. For the moment trans- parent sleeves, often finished on the shoulders by several frills of the same material as the skirt, accompany this style of bodice. Or the sleeves may be cut long on the shoulders, form- ing epaulettes, the closer-fitting portion issuing from the latter and being continued to the wrist. There is certainly a definite charm about these quaint and neat little corsages, quite lack- ing in those styles which gave a round shoul- dered, short-waisted effect. The position of the waist is still a debatable point; it may be high or,low, but both are in moderation, the long line that sometimes descended to the knees has, how- ever, disappeared. Whether the normal line will return remains to be seen, at present the height is a matter of individual preference, therefore every type of figure should be suited. A Much-travelled Nurse.

Very few Englishwomen have seen as much of the terrible side of war as Sister Joan Martin- Nicholson. As soon as possible after the fateful August 3rd, 1914, Miss Martin-Nicholson arrived in Brussels to nurse the Belgian soldiers. The Germans, however, compelled her to assist in the -nursing of their wounded, in the King's Palace; which, before the arrival of the enemy, had in part been converted into a hospital. Later on she was with other British nurses, deported, under an armed escort to Denmark, via Cologne, Hamburg, Essen and the Kiel Canal: She then offered her services to Russia, and went to Petrograd via Finland. The Dowager Empress Marie, to whom she was pre- sented, advised her to go to Warsaw. Subse- quently she undertook service in France, and in a British clearing station behind the lines, and finally was invalided home.

div.head: WE MUST GET AHEAD.
div.p: WE MUST GET AHEAD.
Proposal To Close Museums Criticised By Corpl. Womersley.
SCIENTIFIC EDUCATION
INDISPENSABLE.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—ln reading last Saturday's issue of your paper I noticed a criticism by Mr. Henry Roberts at a Council meeting, of a proposal by Alderman Bennett and the Museum Commit- tee that a letter of protest be sent to the Prime Minister against the closing of museums. Mr. Roberts was strongly of the opinion that no opposition ought to have been offered to the Government's proposal on the gronnd That we ought to retrench all, round. At first .sight, owing to our present troubles, this would appear reasonable, but when we go- into the various ways of retrenchment we find that everything has to be considered on its own merits. We must 'weigh in the -balance the financial saving with the loss to the public welfare or otherwise now and after the war. I would aSk Mr. Roberts whether he has estimated the financial saving the closing of our local Museum would mean, and weighed it in this manner, and also how he would propose to cut down expenditure. To my mind this would mean only an infinitesi- mal saving, for there is only one small item whereby anything could be saved. We could discontinue to keep it open at such times as would require light. No other means offers itself than this, which is infinitesimal, especially note the light nights are beginning. Nobody eligible for our forces could be discharged atm somebody else employed at a cheaper rate. We must also consider that the library and reading- rooms are advisedly left out of the proposal, and would have to be kept open. i Further, it is suggested, as a sort of compen- sation, that museums should still be available, by permission, for students. This brings me to the other side of the balance—the value Of the education lost to the public. Where and Why Germany has Outpaced Us. It is only during the war, and due to it, thac we are at last awakening to the value of a scientific education as compared with our past classical one, which has been weighed in the balance and found wanting. We have only too forcibly been shown that our neglect and under valuation of science has enabled Germany to be so much ahead of,us with ammunition supplies And it is not only in the more industrial sciences that we have been outrun. We have failed to take advantage of the less important means of making us a scientific nation. While German men of science have sought for a use for any 'small discovery, which has' apparently no immediate mse, we have discarded it at once, only to be too eagerly picked up and worked at by our enemies. We are asked to close one of our small but important means Of teaching the value of science to' our young people, who will have to take their places in the industrial world after the war. One concludes that afterwards we are to turn our energies to such things. But, then, we shall only be able to say "Too late!" once again. Germany, we may be sure, is ready to start again where she has left off, and with redoubled energy. We, on the other hand, arf to prepare to start and make up her headway, when the war is over. To win as a scientific nation we must not only be on the same level at the end of the war, but ahead, and be prepared to keep ahead. How are we to do this? There are, of course, numerous ways open to us, but, as I 'only refer above to museums, I will only deal with those. Well, we are certainly not going to gain any- thing by closing such valuable institutions. We must make further use of them instead, to arm ourselves against the industrial war, which will follow this one. It used to be thought that such places were nothing more than storehouses of curiosities. Now we do far more useful work by "their means. They are places of 'education, for value almost on a level with schools am' technical institutes. The Value of Museums.
And now we must even make further use of

them. Now is the time that we must usH them, as all our resources, to amplify the at- tempts that are being made to improve our , position as a scientific country. I may just mention a few things in which they could be put to good educational use—use which -would repay a thousand fold any expense we may go to, and certainly be worth many times any saving effected by closing. Taking agriculture first, we have cereals, of which exhibits of great value, not only to elementary scholars, but to students intending to follow it up as a liveli- hood, could be made showing life history, para- sites, growing, and improvement in quality, made by follbwing scientific methods of cross- breeding and manuring. The value of this is evident when one considers one of our local in- dustrial firms. The growth a -.beet for sugar, and its farming on a commercial scale, inighi also be mentioned. Corning to the manufactur- ing side, what splendidly interesting and in structive educational exhibits could be made for the dye industry, its relationship to the gas works, and, on the other hand, to high explo- sives, which the general public knew nothing of before the war. Besides industries of national importance, local manufactures could also be employed. I read of a museum the _ .

_ other day, of which our esteemed Warring- tonian, Mr. E. E. Lowe, B.Sc., is curator, tackling the question of Infantile Death-rate in a similar, simply, popular, and yet scientific manner. That such things are not done 'more than they are is not due to the willingness or ability of curators, but t 3 false economy. Further expenditure, guided by common sense, is better than any closing of museums. So much, then, for the reasons for or against th proposal. We can only conclude that it is a false economy financially, educationally, and in dustrially. If the Government wishes to retrench let them look out the things which will bring about a big saving, and dith no detrimental after-effect. I couldn't suggest anything better than docking the salaries of M.P.'s. It would yield far more than closing London's museums and 'art galleries. Other sources offer thk3mselves, such as cinema theatres, &c. Out here the men expect that what their sacrifices gain will not be lost by any narrow- sighted policy at home. H. WOMERSLEY, Cpl. R.E., • Hon. Sec. Warrington Field Club. Somewhere in France, March 16, 1916. •

div.p: A STANDING DISGRACE.
Youths' Misbehaviout In The Darkened Main Streets lo
The way adolescents of both sexes conthaet

themselves in Sankey-street and Bridge-street at night is abominable, and each evening, but specially on Sundays, special constables are detailed to look after the interests of peaceful pedestrians, whose difficulty in making progress owing to the darkened streets is greatly accentuated 4 by the presence of these young loungers who persist in forming 'groups and obstructing the footpaths and doorways. When requested to move on they do so only for a few yards and the nuisance is in no way minimised. They are a standing disgrace. At times they move along the street all in a row—firm adher- ents to the collective principle—and jostle every- one who comes in their way. We are pleased to see that the police are taking the matter up, and that several prosecutions have taken place. More are pending.

At the Police Court on Wednesday two youths were charged with disorderly behaviour in Bridge-street on the 11th hist It was stated that the youths, both of whom were under the influence of drink, were stagger- ing about the footpath, and endeavouring to kick young ladies' legs from.under them as they passed by. SATURDAY, MARCH 25, 1916.
THE HOUSING QUESTION AND A DEPUTATION.'

There appears to be much concern in town at the action.of the Street Improvement Com- mittee this week relative to the appointment of a -deputation of three members of the Council and an official to attend a Congress

under the auspices of the National Housing and Town Planning Council, to be held in London on five days in next month. Problems of the home that will confront us after the war are to be coniklered, "more especial') those problems relating to housing and the passibility of adopting new and cheap materials and securing economies in the design of cottages." There can be no doubt that the question of housing will be a difficult one when the war is over. Even now, in the absence on active service and in training of some millions of men, there is , a distinct famine in houses, and very few are being built. There are those who believe that the shortage of houses will, in fact, create a sore in our moral, mental and physical organism. that will out-distance many of the other post- war problems combined. It was an apprecia tion of coming trouble in this direction that induced Alderman James Evans, the chair man of the Health Committee, and those whc supported him, to promote in the Council L resolution which was carried unanimouBl3 three weeks ago, in favour of legislation tc .simplify and cheapen the transfer of land, se as to encourage the building of houses fol the workipg classes.

In these conditions it would naturally bc thought that ,only men with broad minds ane. sympathetic, though practical, inclinations, would be sent to represent Warrington at any conference that has in hand the question of the housing of the people. But the Street Improvement Committee have made what is considered a selection that cannot be said altogether to carry out the ideal they should have set themselves. Alderman Bennett is an enthusiast whose enthusiasm, even now the
days of youth are departing, is apt to carry him into the realms of fairyland; but it has always been such as he that have provided the driving force that has made communities
set. His nomination as one of the deputation is, therefore, satisfactory, and commands approval. in every respect., Councillor Pem- berton; as he showed at the last Council

meeting,- is master of this subject and, though he is a little boisterous and harsh in his methods, he is just the man to second the efforts of the Alderman: the third methber of the deputation should surely have been Alderman James Evans. He does not always approach this question in a manner that seems the proper one, from our.point of view; but he is Chairman of the Health Committee, and as the .one specially charged with the physical well-being of the inhabitants of the town, he ought to be very much in evidence wnenever and wherever this question of housing is to be considered. By the si3lection of Councillor Gough the committee have, we think, com- mitted an error of judgment, which the
General Purposes Committee may feel it A duty to rectify before the constitution of the deputation is submitted to the Council next Tuesday week for confirmation.

div.head: QUESTION. By R. OSSULSTON-RICHE.
div.p: THE QUESTION. By R. OSSULSTON-RICHE.
What can I do to-day? What can you do to-day?— That is the question for you and for me— To silence the guns of the outrageous, Huns In Flanders and France away o'er the sea?
What can we do to-day? That is the question, And one !hat carries an unspoken plea What, what can we do to help the "Boys" through The Hell they are facing for you and fOr me?
What can I do to-day? I that am speaking. I who have served in the patriot's plaoe, And, with sword and gun, my duty have done T'ward God, and my King, and my country's race!
What can you do to-day, ye who will Nov hear Your country's call in her hour of need? If you're healthy and fit-get a service kit, And quit you like men of the Bulldog breed!
What can I do to-day—a verran old and grey— But stand aml wait? Yet in the meanwhile I can surely become to the gloomy and glum The -sunshine born in the birth of a smile.
What can yon do to-day? It conscience make reply • Whoever, you are, whate'er you may be, Man, woman, or boy can help to destroy The mad schweinehunden of Germany. •
What can we do to minimise grief, The widows' tears and the orphans' cry? ' Be up and be doing—their pathway bestrewing— With actions that speak and speaking n'er die.
What can we do to-day? Slog on, and sit tight, For Justice and Honour spells—Victory; Thus the Kaiser's Might must be conquered by Right, And Bondage be crushed by—Liberty!
We can all do something, at least for the cause, Remember each honest endeavour , We make will be known to Him on the throne, When we stand in the great Forever.
Maybe we shall hear, in that vast Beyond— Before, or after peace is restored— Jehovah's—" Well done, faithful servant and son, , Come thou in to the joy of the Lord." ,

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 25, 1916. GERMAN BREAD SUPPLY.I EDUCATION WORKERS. IFORESTERS' CONFERENCE.
Comparison With Consumption . In This Country.
POTATOES FOR WHEAT.
By C. E. PARKER.

The "Daily Telegraph" publishes an interest- ing article by Professor W. J. Ashley, of Bir- mingham, on the German bread supply. The ! facts contained therein are based on informa- tion contained in a book recently published by two eminent Germane, one a statistician, the other a physiologist. Professor Ashley says that the fundamental contention of. the book rests oaths relation between the figures 340 and -200. The first figure, 340, rePresents the number of grammes Of flour consumed daily in the form of , bread by each unit in Germany before the war, the second figure, 200; repreSents the allowance per unit under presdnt war conditions. The 340 grammes appears to me a hi‘'one, and if correct, indie:ates that the klertiwtfis,. before -thy war depended more on bread as food than do our own people, and probably such was the case. Our food is more varied and more meat 4. is and was consumed. A working class family in England, say father and mother and three well-grown children will consume as much as 281 b. of bread per week, while a German family similarly constituted on the 340 figure consumed before the war 351 b. of bread. But the im- portant point of comparison is between the 200 grammes, which we know to be definite, and our unaltered consumption in this country. This 200 grammes would work out on the basis named to 151 b. of bread per week per family, against our 281 b. The quality of the bread would also have to be considered. German bread is now composed largely of potatoes and, other food stuffs, of which the food value is not so great as that of wheat flour. The German writers of this 'book state that "while the diminution of the bread supply may involve a wholesome restriction to overfed people, it means for millions distinct under-nutrition, and that while such a condition of things might have no per- manent effect on the national strength if it only lasted a few months, if it continued it would constitute a great danger."

div.head: GREAT DANGER OF UNDERNUTRITION.
div.p: THE GREAT DANGER OF UNDER- NUTRITION.

• It was expected that the harvest of 1915 would enable the German authorities to increase the allowance provided by bread tickets, and this was done for a time in the ease of those engaged in severe manual work. This extra began iv September, 1915, and was continued until January 10th, 1916. On that day the Govern- ment suddenly announced that it felt itself obliged naturally "only as a measure of pre- caution" to go back to the spring allowance of 200 grammes, with very few exceptions. What was the cause of the Government's change of attitude?

It resulted from the disclosure' of the corn census taken in November, which revealed the fact, that the "harvest of 1915 was considerablx below the average. The weather was, of course, blamed for this, but a more operative cause was the inevitable consequences of war conditions. The land had been starved both of labour and fertilisers. Whatever be the feason of Ger- many reverting to the 200 grammes allowance the fact remains that Germany at present, as far as the staff of life is concerned, can .only make an allowhnce which German physiologists declare means kr "some millions of the people distinct under-nutrition,and constitutes a great danger." It must be remembered that this 200 grammes allowance is not a State gift, but has to be paid for at the prices in force for the time being, whieh, like our own, are much higher than in pre-war times. The bread, therefore, can 'Only be procured by those who have the wherewithal to buy it. Unfortunately the poor of Ger- many, and particularly the families of those who are at the Front, are unable from their small allowance to buy even the scant allowance of 200 grammes, and have to live on inferior food or starve. Look at it hOw we may it is a sad fact that the miseries of war fall hardest on those poor victims who are not primarily respon- sible for the conditions under which they have to suffer.
OUR LACK OF FORESIG-riT.

I do not know—iio one knows—if we will have to adopt methods like the Germans to enforce economy. I consider the authorities are much too slow in anticipating Cue conditions we may ave to face, and safeguarding our resources. The Germans look much further ahead than we do. Many of the restrictions now being put in force ought to have been introduced at least a year ago, and if we had been more foreseeing in these things our economic position would have been very much stronger than it is to-day. There is no doubt a great number of our people are voluntarily exercising strict economy, but there is a minot;ity, and I fear a large one, that has not yet awakened to the needs of Oa, hour, and further and more drastic restrictions ought to be imposed by the Government. We trust, however, that bread will be one of the last things to .be regulated; there is yet a wide field for restrictions in unnecessary things. But even in respect to necessities legal curtailment may have to be introduced, not to the extent to which the Germans have been obliged to go, but in the direction of restricting these things to the extent that they are necessary. Bread itself, if wasted, ceases to become a necessity, that is to the extent of the -waste. Economy has been'urged almost entirely from one standpoint-namely of saving in the form of money to be banked or lent to the Government. There is an aspect of the question that is as important, if not more so—l mean that all saving releases a certain amount of labour which is needed in other directions. I may be allowed to suggest to those who have found their k appeals for economy for the sake of saving money ineffective, that

they would find these appeals more effective if they wbuld explain it in the form of work saved as well as money saved. At any rat' they should not ignore this important part of the question. Everything we buy that is un- necessary means the absorption of a certain amount of labour, and everything of which we deny ourselves means the saving of labour Pn t_rn ged in making these things, and directs this released labour into more useful and necessary channels.

At the monthly meeting of the Warrington Education Committee on Monday evening, Canon Morley Stevenson,. moving a vote of thanks to Councillor Henry Roberta, for his _ _

Other sources of public service were open to Mr. Jolley, and into that work he put his back; in fact, he did not think there was a man in Warrington Ito whom the town owed more for multifarious dt.!.es rendered. (Hear, hear.) The vote was carried amid appttuse. Mr. 3aley said their kindness ans almost overwhelming. He felt that they were not only working all together in a great public cause, but all together in a friendly spirit. div.p: North-Western,Federation Meets In Warrington.
TO-DAY'S VISITORS.

The representatives of the North-Western Federation, Ancient Order of Foresters, will assemble this afternoon, and hold their amnia conference in the Town Hall at 3 o'clock, which has been lent far the occasion by His Worship the Mayor, who is a brother Forester, and has always taken great interest in Friendly Society work in the town.

This is the second time of the •Federation meeting in Warrington. The first meeting was held 10 years ago, in September, 1905. The Federation was inaugurated 21 years ago at Chester., It was the :putcome of what was pre- viously known as the Manchester and District Union. On the late Bro. John Bowler relin- quishing his office as secretary of the Manchester District, no one seemed to take any interest in the Union, whereupon the Chester District, who were seeking High Court ,honours at that time, called a representative meeting of all Dis- tricts and Courts within a radius of 30 miles,of Chester (including the Manchester District Union), meeting in Chester- on a Saturday afternoon in June, 1905. .The outcome of the meeting resulted in the reformation of the Man- chester Union under the title of the North- Western Federation Ancient Order of Foresters The Federation extends over a large area, in- cluding five counties, namely, Cimberland, ILancashire, Cheshire, Flintshire, and Derb /- shire. Within the area there are 30 Districts and '321 Courts' with 42926 members. The,Dis- tricts are worth £35,635 in funeral funds, anti the Courts are worth 2423,133, making a com- bined total of District -and Court funds of 2458,768.

div.head: Work of the Federation.
div.p: The Work of the Federation.
The objects of the Federation are to discuss questions relating to the work of the Order, and what will be for the advantage of the Districts

and Courts, also business that is to be brought before the annual conference of the High Court, held in August each year, with a view to com- bined action of the representatives of the Courts and Districts within the federated area. The. Federation has been instrumental in assisting many Districts *to secure the holding, of the High Courts, which has had a tendency to further the interests of Fbrestry in the neighbourhood where the High Court was being held. It has also been able to help many mem- bers to' secure seats on the Executive and other positions of honour in connectioa with the Order. Brother G. W. Smith, Past High Court Secretary and Past District Chief Ranger, of Manchester, has had the dis- tinguished honour of beifig secretary .to the Federation since it was inaugurated, and he still holds that responsible position. . Honour to Warrington Forester.

The meeting teKlay ist under the presidency of Bro. Maybury, Past. Thst. Chief Ranger of the Warrington District. At the last meeting of the Federation (which was held in Manchester) it was decided to honour the Chairman by holding a meeting in the district of which he was a member. Brother Maybury has been president for two years in.succession (no other member having had such an honour). He has been a member since its formation, and has attended meetings all over the area, including Barrow- nessPw Accrington, Clitheroe. Burnley. Wigan, Chester, Manchester, Flint, Stockport, and many other districts where the meetings have been held. The committee who have been instructed by the District to make arrangements for the meeting, consist of the District Officers, to- gether with the Chairman of the Federation and Brother W. Hipkiss. Arrangements have been made for tea for the repreeentAtivt,s at the ' Winmarleigh Cafe at the close of -the meeting. I The District is looking forward to having a, good representation of delegates, and trusts the results of the meeting will be beneficial to the interests not only of the Warrington Districts of Foresters, hut to all the kindred societies in the district.

div.head: "CHEERFUL AND FIT."
div.p: "CHEERFUL AND FIT."
South Lancashires " Resume Business " After Rest.
Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, Town Clerk, his this week received the following letter from Cap- tain Sydney Boast, of the 2nd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment:—
"18th March, 1916.

"Dear Sir,—l have to thank you very much for your kind letter if 16th February. 1 delayed answering it until the cigarettes and tobacco yOu mentioned had arrived—they ar- rived safely on Bth March, and were duly dis- tributed amongst the men of the battalion, who are all very grateful to their friends at home who so kindly remember them in suoh a suitable manner. On behalf of all ranks I send, througa you, sincere thanks for the smokes.' Whoa they arrived we were still at rest, but under orders to move to a. new area. We started on the morning of the 10th, and, thanks to the gift .from Warrington, everyone startea with a good ration of smokes. We have been march- ing almost daily since, and have just arrive 1 in our new area. We are now halted; and 1 expect one more march will bring us into tho fighting area' once more. All ranks of th 3 battalion are very cheerful and wonderfully We have had a good rest, and everyone ha thoroughly appreciated it. Battalion Win Brigade Cup.

"During the time the battalion has been out of the trenches every opportunity has been takea for games and all kinds of recreation. Com- panies held smoking concerts in their billets, battalion sports were held, mid we had several 'cross-country ' races. In my last letter 1

Mentioned the inter-company football competi- tion—our best company was 'D,' but they wer.? defeated by a company of another battalion in the brigade.' "Towards the end of our rest, brigade sports. took place. These were a great success,.- and thoroughly enjoyed by everyone. The events were mainly • tam' events, and, of a total of nine of these events, the battalion took .four first and. four second prizes. Points were also awarded .as follows:—Vive for a win, three fo; a -second place, and one for a third place, and the-battalion adjudged to be the winning battalion was awarded a silver cup. We were fortunate enough to win this, and• it has•since been sent to the Depot at Warrington for Safe custody. Naturally we are all v...,ny proud of having secured this cup, and I. am sure our many friends at home, especially those in our local district, will be very pleased too.

div.head: Farther South.

"I expect we shall be on the move again to., morrows and possibly before this reaches, yog we shall have resumed ' business ' again. . are much farther south- than when I last wrote to you, and we have passed through some very firm country during. out marches. . We have. had 'a deal of snow since I last wrote- to you,, but during the past couple of weeks, especially while we hair() been marching, the weather has been exceptionally good. • "I have no more news which the censor will permit to send you this time, so will conclude: with every "geed Wish to -yourself' and all 'old friends.—Yours very sincerely,• - SYDNEY T. div.head: TALENTED SOLDIERS
div.p: TALENTED SOLDIERS
Entertain Fellow-Wounded At Winwiek.
WAR-BABY SCENE.

A trick fell to• every effort essayed by the wounded soldiers (now, happily, convalescent) at their concert in the Lord Derby -Military Hospital, Winwick, on Tuesday afternoon. The entertainers risked "abundance" ! and carried off all honours unchallenged, while doctors in khaki, boys in blue, and nurses in grey, sat delighted. Since their last full-dress appearance these soldier-entertainers have added two to their number, making them sixteen in all. They have also got a baby of about fourteen stone. Generally, they still sport Pierrot costumes, and the only difference rile noticed in the habits of those acting as ladies was that instead 'of black they were wearing red stockings. Their comrades in France must have been de- tailing Paris fashions, or, perhaps, they them- selves have been taking an interest in the ladies' pages of " Pathe's Gazette" at the Cinema. The effect was picturesque. Corpora/ Pearson (one of the ladies) has lost none of his sauciness and naivete; nor has Private Huggins (another); while Private Pearce (a new-comer) has absorbed the spirit of elfish femininity to the last drop. He scored a great success with his singing of "Just a little love."

Picturesqueness and novelty abounded throughout the programme. The stage looked like a conservatory during the singing of "Tulip Time" by Corporal Hodge, Private Pollir,gton and Lady Hugtins executing grace- ful dancing movements, to the accompaniment of piano and mandoline. Among the palm trees and in the palms of the hands of the chorus cut-tulips shone brightly.

div.head: WAR-BABY.
div.p: WAR-BABY.

A piquant episode was that of "Hullo, Baby." Lady Pearson walked about singing, an im- provised nurse sat on on a garden seat, attended by a devoted soldier, and a very bonny baby overcrowded a perambulator, looking a perfect picture of contentment in his white linen hat and frock (bedecked with blue ribbons) and with a dummy-teat closely encircled by his rosy lips. All went well until the last verse, when one imp robbed the youngster of his rubber comforter, and a great yell rent the air. The way that child cried was wonderful. Even Teddy Slingsby, when he realises he has been disinherited, will not cry more whole- heartedly. His face contorted and expanded, his cheeks glistened with tears, and his mouth stretched from ear to ear, like the line of a diameter across a circle. But it was only for a moment or two, the curtain being lowered after tle surprise had been enjoyed. One hadn't time to see if the poor kid had cut his teeth.

A part-song, "When. the Angelus is ringing,' was rendered most excellently by Rifleman Jones, Corporal Hodge, Lance-Corporal Mer- chant, Rifleman Gordon (late of the Carl Rosa Company), Corporal Buckley, Corporal Pear- son and Private Caldwell. Private Hughes triumphed through his whistling of "My Hero" t" Chdeolate Soldier") and "Row me on the river, Romeo"; and other excellent items were: "Mississippi Lou," by Sergeant Fishbrook; "The sunshine of your smile," hy Private Redfern; "My Moon," and "Vauxhall Way," by Lance-Corporal Merchant; "I'm Love," by Lady Pearson; "Pack up your troubles in your old kit-bag," by Private Kerrigan (a rare comedian, this man); "Bedouin's Love Song," Rifleman Jones; "Tip- top Tipperary Mary," by Private Pollington; "The Only Way," by Lady Huggins, assisted by Private Pollington for the dancing; and "They didn't believe me," by Corporal Pear- son and Lance-Corporal Merchant.

div.head: SUGGESTION.
div.p: A SUGGESTION.

By W. STEWART ROYSTON.

Looking at a Victoria Cross cin the breast of a soldier does it ever occur to the reader that its value is little more than the smallest silver coin of the Realm? Yet it is the most coveted honour a brave soldier can possess. A millionaire with his pile of gold would find it utterly impossible to buy the highest tribute to our heroes on the battlefield. It is an honour beyond the reach of a bribe, for only by unflinch- ing courage and daring and suffering can it be obtained. If it is through suffering and trial we are made more thoughtful for others, then from King George down: to the humblest of his subjects the finest example has been shown to the whole world!
SPLENDID SPIRIT OF SELF-SACRIFICE.

In our home circle we have seen mothers' and sisters' fingera busy making and preparing cow- forta for "someone's loved laddie " the trenches, as though it were tor our own selves, and there seems- only one .desire to get them finished and sent off to the " brave" without delay. In tens of thousands of homes has this splenclid spirit of self-denial been going on sizte the outbreak of the terrible war. One could with little difficulty fill columns in support of the opinion that the war of 1914-11 i has brought- out the best of the British race. Two instances will suffice, and are worth recording in "The Examiner." in a big city there dwells a 'lady to-day whose health has been far from robust, yet she has sent a rountless.number of comforts for the body and cheer for the mind to men in the trenches, as well as to "Lonely Harry," a prisoner interned in Holland since the fall .of Antwerp! Even when the effects of the war reduced her income, rather than discontinue her splendid work she obtained a temporary position as a lady gardener! • The same spirit has been shown in another way by a friend whose motor car has gone week after week for eighteen months to the Lord Derby War Hos- pital, and very many wounded soldiers. Colonials as well as our own countrymen, have been taken out for health-giving drives and a refreshing tea, and then safely back to their "haven of Peace' Long after the terrible strife is over and the brave recovered from their wounds will they carry happy memories of "their friend and mine." whose motor car brought the V.C. to my home in the quiet eanntryside

This visit was entirely due to my efforts to raise funds to buy walking sticks for the wounded soldiers in our military hospitals who are in great need of them, and almost the first to receive one was the V.C. How full of grati- tude this brave man was for the doctors and "sisters" who had done' so much to heal his wounds! What a modest hero he was to have found more interest in examining the tributes which have come to me for services done for 'qthers. and more especially he admired the beautiful little medal which the then Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph), of Warrington, pre- sented to myself "to commemorate the Corona- Hon of King George and Queen Mary," for he snoke about these with seemingly more interest than of his own heroic deeds! "There are thousands deserve a V.C.—you do" said he.

div.head: V.C. SHARES HIS HONOUR.
div.p: V.C. SHARES HIS HONOUR.

It is quite evident that we have in this brave soldier the right type of V.C., for he feels that this coveted honour is being worn on his breast for the heroic deeds of his comrades who wer* roused up to follow him to victory through shot and shell and poisonous gases! What a fine spirit it Was to hear that when somtone asked him if he was not proud of his Vitoria Cross he replied "My wife and kiddies will be." True it is that a brave man wears the V.C. to represent the heroic deeds of his mates, just as the man with an M.P. behind his name represents the opinion of the majority of those who have /sent him to represent them in the House of Com- mons!

As an Englishman one could not help wishing that we were as " clannish " and as ready to show pride in heroic deeds as those who live across the Tweed, for when the proposed visit was known among my Scottish friends—and as friends they are gems in loyalty I—a message cam 6 from Edinburgh as follows . .

"Tell the V.C. that Scotland is very proud of him, and is sending all the men she can to help in the war. 'I know, as a Derby canvasser that she is' doing well, and we shall not leave in the lurch the brave who are saving the Empire in, the trenches, at such a sacrifice to himself. I feel sure Lancashire boys will not lag behind." I had also the pleasure of handing to the V.C. a large shortbread cake sent by a lady friend in Portobello, and while he was examin- ing the beautiful way it was decorated in Scottish fashion, and tied up with the regi- mental ribbons, another parcel was -sent up to him from another kind lady friend of Scottish descent. When the V.C. saw on opening it con- tained cigarettes he exclaimed: "Theta() are *hat we like in the trenches. I would rather have scone without a meal a dai, than be without the cigarettes." So, reader, do not forget the hint! Before this modest hero took hi, s departure and what had been a memorable and happy visit, was brought to a close it was mentioned .to him that I was an Associate of the "Pansy League," and that it was our aim to live up to the promiqe
—"to be thoughtful of others." So a sealed Dackage was handed to the V.C. with instruc- tions it was not to be opened, but must be given to his wife on reaching his Mime in Scotland.

div.head: FOUND IN THE TRENCHES.
div.p: FOUND IN THE TRENCHES.
Antiquities Which Soldiers Are Digging Up.
BY ARTHUR MOUNFIELD.

. Archaeologists are getting a lot of quiet Satis- faction out of the war. They may deplore-it as much as other people, but to get so much dig- ging done for nothing, and without asking is almost too good to be tiii`e. If the antiquarians of Europe had asked that •four or ve theueand 'mike of deep trenches shetild be cut throaghlhe historic regions Of Macedonia, Mesopotamia and the _islands of. the JEgean,: it would • have been discovered that the Government could not. pos- sibly afford 'Bach-foolish luxury. But the dig- ging has been done, and on the whole done very 'well. --It is true thatthe average "Torgmy" thinks that he is digging up gravestones when he is bringing out a Mesopotamian idol or a Greek statue, but he has wisdom enongh to put the fragments aside, and in due course the archaeolo- gist will. scan them and tell what has been found. "Tommy" won't read his findings, but the rest of the world will, and somebody will be wiser. • Though it is too soon to talk about the exact nature of the discoveries, it will interest otir readers to learn something of the places in which wholesale trench digging is going on. . Beginning in the West, the English and French trenches run through the scenes ofcmany- famous mediaeval happenings. • At goissons the French soldiers have uncovered the foundations of an ancient church endowed by the famous King Clovis, the first Frankish chieftain who became a Christian. Architects will have a rich time by and by studying these old stones. For the present the neighbourhood is; ,in soldier's language, "very unhealthy."

Relics of King Darius, As we, travel eastward the objects discovered increase in antiquity. From the furtheet east at Mesopotamia comes the news that the soldiers have found at Kut-el-Armama a series of won- derfully carved sculptures, of King Darius, vrhichirecord his conquest of Babylon, the great- est city of that distant day. The armies in the Balkans are fighting over territory which was successively civilised by Alexander the,Great and by the Roman Empire, but •which has since fallen into semi-barbarism. Alexander, it may be recalled, was King of Mace- donia in his early years, and the soldiers are now digging through the foundations of the cities he founded and the fortifleations he built. This is an extremely interesting field that has never been fully explored by archa3ologists. The eastern side of the. Adriatic, for which Italy is now fighting, was an important part of the Roman Empire not far removed from Rome itself. It is curious to reflect that a country which ranked with the foremost in Europe should be the most barbarous part of Europe to- day. When, the archEeolpgist goes over the an- tiquities dug up—and there is an amazing num- ber of them—he will tell us much of the days when Rome ruled the world. •

The Russian Army has recovered many fine relies Of the past from its trenches. Greek civilisation extended far into Russia in ancient times, and many sites of buried and forgotten cities lie there. Some of these have been opened up by the soldiers' spades. and curious and beautiful statues and remarkable jewellery of gold and rare stones sparkle in the light after two and a half millenniums.
