div.head: " Winged Victory" From Gallipoli.
div.p: A " Winged Victory" From Gallipoli.

If there had but been time it would have been a good thing to give the Dardanelles forces a few lessons in ancient history. For they have been to the shores where ancient Troy was situ- ated, and a little knowledge would have given them some clue to the scraps of statuary and fragments of temples which made trench dig- ging so troublesome a process. One lucky wielder of the pick at Gallipoli extracted a fine marble image, which is discovered to be a winged statue of Victory in the best Athenian style, and which probably was carved to com- memorate a victory of the Athenians in the Peloponnesian war. If that trench maker is 3pared to visit the British Museum after the war he will be proud to see his piece of marble among the nation's treasures. A similar piece of good fortune came to the French in the island of Lemnos. This Greek island has been used as a base in the Dardan- -2,11es operations. Readers of mythology may re- member that in the story of the search for the Golden Fleece the Argonauts came to the island 9f Lemnos to discover that it was inhabited by women only. The women it was said had sud- denly murdered all the men in revenge for ill- treatment, but they were so impressed by the gentle bearing of the new corners that they re- ceived them to their midst.
Upon this island is an ancient site covered with broken columns and fragments of brick and marble.

The place is known to the 'Greeks as Palaio- polis or "Old City." In all probability it is the site of .the ancient Greek city of Hephaestia, said to have been founded by Hephaestus, the god of fire, and son of Zeus and Hera. When Greece flourished this city had 68,000 inhabit- ants, a larger population than Athens. Digging., here some French soldiers found a beautiful statue of the Greek god Eros. Unearthing A Greek Statue. This is how the circumstance was described by the officer in charge:— "Our men who were digging the trench sud- denly came upon the floor of a large building, evidently -a temple or palace. I was looking at them carelessly when one of them said, 'This sounds hollow.' That attracted my attention, and I became excited by the idea that in the course of our, duties we might discover some precious relic. I told our -men that they might come upon a Greek amphora filled with pieces of gold, and they dug away with increased energy. "Suddenly a man with a pick cried, Here is something solid. I caught a glimpse of a round piece of marble. I thought it was the base of column. 'Dig gently,' I ordered. "Suddenly a white human shoulder came into view. I called all my comrades. Quick, quick —a statue!' They couli hardly believe it. The duties of military operations had led us to this spot, where we found a masterpiece of Greek art hidden since ancient times!

"We proceeded with the greatest care to ex- tract the statue. Alas! it had no head! In a short time we had disengaged the torso frpm the soil. The arms had been broken off and were missing. One leg was complete to the left knee. The greater part of the right leg was missing. The statue was about two-thirds of natural size and weighed over 300 pounds. Upon the back were the remains of wings that had been broken off.

"It was a statue of a young Greek god, a yoUth of the most exquisite beauty, comparable with the Hermes of Praxiteles. We decided that it was a statue of Eros, the god of love. "We were so excited that we could not stop to eat at the customary lunch hour. We were anxious to recover the rest of the statue—the arms, the legs, the wings. At the end of an hour we came upon an ,object that gave promise of being one of the missing fragments. It proved to be the right thigh. Soon we dis-. covered the calf of the same limb. The sun *as fearfully hot„ and our men were growing ex- hausted and caked with dust. We worked on arduously until dark, but without finding any more of the missing pieces of the statue. " We .were, however, able to obtain an inter- esting piece of evidence as to the nature of the disaster that put an end to the ancient city of Hephaestia. Opinion among historians has been divided' between the view that it was destroyed by an earthquake, and that it was sacked by the Turks when they first began to overrun the Greek dominions. We decided that it had been destroyed by an earthquake. In the corner of this we found the skeleton of an ancient Greek bull, or cow. This we took to be evidence of the earthquake. It was not likely that the marauding Turks would have driven the animal here in their destructive raid. They wont& have eaten it. The animal had evidently taken refuge here, terrified by the earthquake, and had been buried among the ruins." The French officer presented his find to the Greek authorities. It was his request that the statue should be placed in a Greek museuni with the inscription: -

• "Found by the officers and soldiers of the Dardanelles Expeditionary Corps at Palaipolis, in Lemnos, in 'the campaign against Germany, Anirtria-nungary and Turkey, 1915." : liabels with a similar inscription will soon be timiliar in all the museums of Europe,, and his- torians Who look back upon the war will prob- ably declare that it gave us more Eastern an-. tiquisies than all the previous century of re- search and digging.

The Rev. G. Vale Owen gives many extracts from letters sent bz oriord men stationed in many parts of the world, on land and sea, in this month's ". Orford Parish Magazine." From these letters we make tho following quotations:

div.head: IN THE BEST OF SPIRITS.
div.p: IN THE BEST OF SPIRITS.

"However," says one - correspondent after describing a military cemetery, "you are not to think we are at all doleful; rather the reverse. It is a sight to see an infantry battalion coming from the trenches covered with mud, but apparently in the best of spirits. They come out for a rest and are soon playing football matches, as if there was no war within a hundred miles."

"Casualties occur," says another writer, "and it is a sad thing to see one and then another of the old familiar faces disappear from the regiment. But, after all, it is only like life in peace time speeded up."

div.head: HOW WARRINGTON WOULD LOOK AFTER
div.p: HOW WARRINGTON WOULD LOOK AFTER
BOMBARDMENT.

"The first thing that strikes one on entering such a place [a town that had been heavily shelled] is the deserted fook," says a writer in France. "It is easy imagine the path 2 there must have been wh-:n the shells com- menced to fall. Houses with the fronts knocked in, others with the sides taken away, and all the 'household effects visible. Then a row knocked absolutely down, and one house quite untouched. A fine church smashed full of holes and heaps of mosaic from its front lying -all around it, and what had probably been a cafe just a heap of broken glass and bricks. A few people still live on amongst the ruined homes, but most of the inhabitants have gone.

"It would give you some idea if you imagine Warrington with Holy Trinity Church a mass of ruins, the Parish Church with its fine steeple knocked off, and the fabric pitted with holes: one side of Bridge-street a heap of stones, and the other side having only a few houses stand- ing; Sankey-street and Market-place just a huge heap of ruins from which soldiers waded up bricks to repair the roads and to make standings for their horses. All down Horsemarket-street and Orford-lane you are to imagine all the houses pitted with holes, and only one or 'two small shops open. The Queen's would be just tottering structure of four walls, full of holes. and the whole place around there would 'look as if shaken by some great earthquake. If you could imagine the old town so. it would give you an exact idea of what a heavily shelled town is like. One can imagine, then, what the war has meant to France, and what it would mean if' England were exposed to the full force, of Ger- man strafing." WAITING FOR BULGARS.

"THE EXAMINER" REPRESENTATIVE.
The Examiner" has new sent four members of its literary staff to the Colours; and the work of covering district areas is becoming increasingly difficult. t
To assist -us in keeping the supply of Lyinm news up to its present high level we have • engaged the services of
Mr. S. D. Moston,
Booth's Hill, who has already done his bit and earned his discharge from the Army; and we shall be deeply indebted to friends if they will. give him any assistance that lies in their power.
Mr. Moston is well-known to Lymm people, and it is with every confidence that we put our news interests in the village largely in his hands.

Golfing A ccident.—A somewhat serious acci- dent occurred on the golf course last Saturday. Miss Eva Hatton, a well-known local school teacher, was in the act of watching her opponent make a drive. She got a little too close, with the result that when the club was swung over the shoulder it caught, her a nasty knock in the face, which stunned her for a time. We are pleased to say that at the time of writing she is progressing favourably.

Mouth Organ Fund.—With such a musical man at the head of affairs as Mr. William Cooke, one cannot be surprised if this fund exceeds all expectations. In order to help it along he gave an organ recital after evening service on Sunday. Amongst the pieces selected were the "Prelude" and "Fugue," by J. S. Bach; "Elegie," by H. W. Ernst; and the Servian National Anthem, which were ren- dered in a masterly manner. Mrs. Wilson, a well-known local singer, delighted the audience with a solo, "Come, unto Me." A collection was made at the door at the close.

Sergeant J. H. Moston Recovering.—Sergt. J". H. Moston, a member of the local "Terriers," who is at present an inmate of the Mater Hos- pital, Belfast, suffering from: a nervous break- down, writing to his aunt, Mrs. Geo. Davies, of Booth's Hill, states:—" I am very glad to say I am feeling a deal better and am well on the road to recovery. We are having splenilid weather here, and we get out very often. I don't think I shalt be ,very long before I am able to see you, for I don't suppose they will keep me here much longer. It is St. Patrick's Day to-morrow, and we are celebrating it with a dance and concert in thtv large hall adjoining the hospital, so we are sure to have a good time." Sergeant J. H. Moston, prior to the war, was employed by the Post Office as postman.

The Late Private Samuel Jennings.—Mr'. William Jennings, Moston-street, Newfield, ha, this week received a War Office communicatioi confirming the report which we published last week to the effect that her son, Private Samuel Jennings, King's Liverpool Regiment, has becn killed in action. A letter received from ho' younger son, Private James Jennings, of tht 1/sth Manchester Regiment, who is with tha Mediterranean Expeditionary Forces, says he is in the best of health, though in a very hot place. He -praises the food he is receiving, and adds:." There are only three of us in the tent— Billy Wilkinson, another Pal, and myself—so you can bet we did justice to the bread anti butter, herrings in tomato sauce. fish paste, and jam."

Irish Soldiers' Flag 'Day.—Friday (St. Pat- rick's Day) and Saturday were observed in Lymm as Flag Day for the Irish soldiers. The effort put forth was well supported by an earnest body of collectors, ladies' and gentle- men taking part, together with some of the scholars (past and present) from the schools in the neighbourhood. The sum raised reached the gratifying amount of £6 Os. Bd. All who took part in the effort are to be congratulated on the very satisfactory result, and the Organising Committee tender their hearty thanks to all who rendered such valuable assistance, and to the public for their generous response. The collectors were: Mrs. Parmiter, Miss Cole, Miss E. Dalton, Mr. Cole, Mr. F. E. Evans, Esther Soares, Gladys Watson, Elsie Odber, Ruth Wilson, Daisy Davies, Mona Seed and Winnie Hills. The total• amount collected in Altrincham, Sale, Knutsford and Lymm is £l5O. .

Volunteers' Sealed Handicap.—" Good shooting is the first step to proficiency." So say the mem- bers of the Lymm Platoon .I.Cheshire Volunteer Regiment). Some shooting of real merit was witnessed at their handicap on the range adjoin- ing' the Drill Hall on Monday and Tuesday. The prizes, generously given by Platoon Commander G. R. Williamson and Messrs. W. N. Moles- ' worth and J. T. Milne, consisted of silver flower vase, a silver-mounted set of carvers, and a silver-plated cruet. The successful winners were:-1 Pte. W. E. Hillier, who made a score of 84 points with a handicap of 15 points, which made him 99 points; 2, Sergt. S. D. Moston (handicap 4), which made him 98; 3 (tie) Sergt. Lister Farrar and Pte. T. Done (handicap 4), 97. This prize was shot off for, the result being in favour of Sergeant Farrar. The prizes were presented to the successful competitors by Platoon Commander G.E. Williamson, who con- gratulated the winners. Sergeants Moston and Farrar and Private Hillier suitably replied.

Wounded Soldiers Entertained.—Some people think that the wounded soldiers at the Brook- field Military Hospital have a monotonous time, but such is not the case. On interviewing a member of the hospital committee, our repre- sentative found that concerts, whist drives and theatre parties occur several times a week. On Saturday the patients were treated to a splendid -concert organised by Mrs. J. H. Holt, of Killodam, Cherry-lane. Songs were rendered by Mrs. Booth, the well-known Warrington singer, and Miss Blackburn, whose fine songs evoked considerable applause. Miss H. Hammon, of Knutsford, delighted the audience with her fancy dancing,- her graceful performances leav- ing nothing to be desired. Miss F. Holt. who has won several musical honours, contributed violin solos in finished style, and Mr. W. Mort kept the audience in good humour by his Lanca- shire readings, which never fail to bring forth peals of laughter. Miss Jessie Holt, officiated at the piano. At intervals soldiers contributed items themselves, and so put the finishing touch to a splendid evening's entertainment.

James Taylor Returns.—Private James Tay- lor, the head of a fine patriotic Lymm family, has this week been discharged by the Army authorities as "too old." He has thirty-two years' service to his credit, thirty of whichi he spent .as a' Regular soldier in the 2nd j Battalion South Lancashire Regiment The remaining two he served during the present campaign as al member of the 10th Battalion ,South Lancashire Regiment. On calling at his residence at West Hyde, Newfiekis, our repre- sentative found him looking the picture of health, and certainly in the best of spirits. On inquiring about his Army career, .he found out that he had seen service in Gibraltar, Malta, China, and South Africa, and had had some very weird experiences. He was one of the salvage men sent out to South Africa directly after the war for the purpose of burying the dead. • His son, Private James Taylor, jun., it will be remembered, was the first local Territorial to be wounded, and through this wound lost the entire use of his left arm. He is at present engaged on munition work. A step-son, Corporal Henry Brookes, also of the local Territorials, wais some • time ago awarded the Order of ,St. George, 2nd Clasp, for heroic ambulance work whilst under fire.

div.head: SIGNALLER CLARKE.
div.p: SIGNALLER CLARKE.
Statham Gardener Dies From
Shrapnel Wounds.

Mr. George Clarke, of the Nursery Gardens, Poole-lane, Statham, has this week received news to the effect that his son, Signaller Frank Clarke, has died of wounds received in France. News was first received through the medium of .a letter sent by a sister at one of the base hos- pitals, stating that he had been admitted into hospital on the 15th of March, suffering from serious shrapnel wounds in the body. This was closely followed by another letter from..the same source, which stated that he passed away on the 16th. War With Luck To Finish In Three Months.

Sapper Percy Clare, of the Royal Engineers: whose home address is Booth's Hill, has this week written to his mother to the effect that he has rejoined his regiment. Sapper Percy Clare, it will be remembered, went out to the Front fifteen months ago, along with the local "Terriers," but after about•thre months he volunteered along with his cousin, Sapper Joseph Clare, for mining work with the R.E.'st and has been with this Corps ever since. div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

Wesley Guild.—The closing social gathering of the winter session was held on Thursday evening in the Schoolroom, when a good num- ber of members and friends assembled. The Rev. Percy Meson (pastor) opened -the proceed- ings with prayer. Mr. H. Brereton presided. Miss Vera Jones contributed a song, which was much enjoyed, and also took part in the duet "Down the Vale" with Miss H. Evans. Mrs. Percy Meson delighted the audience with a well-executed recital, whilst considerable amuse- ment was caused by the humorous recitals of Mr. Sansom. A pretty action song by the girls of the Band of Hope was much appreciated. Refreshments were served by members of the Social Committee, with Mrs. Whitfield as pre- sident and Mr. H. Ditchfield as secretary, who most successfully carried out the arrangements. The remainder of the evening was devoted to games, in which, old and young entered most heartily. Miss Turner was the accompanist.

Adult School Dramatic Reading.—On Monday evening the members of the above school gave a dramatic reading of Shakespeare's "Julius Cesar." They had the assistance of Mr. Alfred Perris, who took the part of Brutus, owing to the original exponent being called away at the last moment. The performance showed that' tte memhe-; had made a careful study of the play. 'ln ordinary dress, with book in hand, without scenery of any description, and without the "business" with which actors— professional and amateur—are apt to overload a play, the performers gave an intelligent ren- dering of the scenes, and contrived to bring out their dramatic interest. At the outset a slight degree of nervousness was apparent which caused some faulty diction, but this trouble was soon overcome and the performers settled down comfortably into their parts. The ripe experience of Mr. Perris clothed .the char- acter of Brutus with dignity and power, and the example of "the noblest Roman of them all" helped the novices to realise that they themselves were for the nonce "noble Romans," whether they were senators or sooth- sayers; servants, messengers, cobblers, car- penters or generals. And, as it happened, one man might be all—or nearly all—these persons, for, in order to keep the cast within reasonable limits, it was necessary to give a number of minor parts to the same performer.—The read- ing was the outcome of a lecturette recently delivered in the school on "Brutus." A lectur- ette fails in its main object if it does not whet the appetite for more, and in regard to any of Shakespeare's plays the most 'instructive and exhilarating mode of following the chase is to read the play aloud and thus discover some- thing of its inner meaning. Shakespeare does not yield up his treasures to the cursory metier; the neeersity for careful re- hearsal of his plays. The recognition of this by no means painful necessity accounts for the 3uccess of the reading at Stockton Heath.

div.head: CRUEL HUSBAND.
div.p: A CRUEL HUSBAND.
Has "Good Time," And Wife Gets Separation Order.

At the Borough Police Court on Tuesday, Anne Sherratt, 27, Orford-lane, applied for a separa- tion order from her husband, Frank Sherratt, 34, Tilley-street, on the grounds of persistent cruelty. He pleaded not guilty. Mr. T. S. Steel, who appeared for complainant; said he was surprised to hear defendant plead not guilty, for he (Mr. Steel) could call several witnesses to whom defendant had admitted that he had been cruel to his wife, and had begged for forgiveness. The parties had been. married five years, and there were two children. De- fendant had been in the habit of going out after dinner on Saturdays and not coming back until the early hours of Sunday morning. On Satur- day, the 11th inst., the defendant returned from work about five o'clock in a very drunken con- dition. His wife asked him. for some money, which he refused to bye her, and, getting on to the sofa, slept until 7.30, n hen he was again asked for money, but he refused and went out. Although his wife followed, she lost sight of him, and when she went back home she found him there. He commenced to grin at her. His wife again asked him for money, and he struck her in the mouth and cut both her lips. He then left the house and did not return until Sunday morning, when he was drunk. He afterwards demanded his breakfast, and when told there was none for him, he again assaulted his wife. Hearing-the noise, a neighbour went in and separated them. The defendant. how- ever, assaulted his wife later in the day. He went out and returned at midnight, when he said "he had had a good time." Defendant had I been seen in Crosfield-street and near the Market with strange women.
Poker Used In Defence.

Mrs. Sherratt bare out Mr. Steel's statement, and added that her husband had told her to " blow out her brains" with a gun which they had in the house. Answering the defendant, complainant admitted striking him with a poker. Defendant alleged that his wife bad struck him on the head with a knife. Several witnesses said defendant had admitted to them that he had been cruel to his wife. Inspector Wainwright (N.S.P.C.C.) said defend- ant had also admitted that fact to him, and had asked him to smooth matters over, adding "There are faults on both sides." Defendant, ho produced fragments of a broken jug with which' he alleged his wife had hit him, said he earned 455. per week and war bonus. He gave his wife 30s. per week, and himself bought all the clothes. The allegations his wife had made, ho contended, were a "pack of lies."
A separation order, with 255. per week alimony, was granted, along with advocate's fee. Defendant was also ordered to pay the costs.

An introduction To The Economic History Of England.
I. The Middle Ages. By E. Lipson, M.A. London: A. and C. Black. 7/6 net.

The study of English Economic History has made such rapid progress, and works dealing with its special periods and aspects have been published in such numbers in recent years, that it is well to have the main facts and conclu- sions gathered together in a single work. This volume is not the first attempt that has been made in this direction, but Mr. Lipson has had an advantage over mans 61 his predecessors in, that, in addition to the older sources of evi-' deuce, he has been able to avail himself of the masa of new material, auchns the Patents Rolls, Litter Books, and Town Records, which has recently been made accessible to the investiga- tor. These documents furnish us with valuable information on many points that were formerly very obscure, and in not" a few cases render necessary a reversal of the judgment of past historians. Mr. Lipson has not been slow to utilise these newer sources of evidence, with the result that he is able to prove untenable many of the views vihich held the field up to the publication of the present vehime. Mr. Lipson traces our "economic history from the period when the taanoiiiil system was in, operation right up to the organisation of indus- try and foreign trade at the end of the Middle Ages. Considerable discussion is devoted to the problem of the origin of the manor, the various theories of which being summarised and com- pared, Mr. Lipson does not decide in favour of any one of the conflicting theories, holding that "no theory of the manor is tenable which lays stress upon one aspect to the entire exclusion of the rest." The various problems connected with the tenurial holdings under the manorial system, the question of slavery, the peasants' revolt, the agrarian revolution, the growth of' towns, and fairs and markets, all these matters are discussed with a wealth of illustration, and in a manner which leave nothing to be desired.

'Craft Guilds. • The longest, and one of the most interesting, chapters of the book is devoted to a searching Investigation into the constitution and func- tions of the Craft Guilds, which were a charac- teristic feature of the later Middle Ages. Super- ficial acquaintance with the guild system tempts one to compare it with modern trade unionism. and, indeed, as Mr. Lipson admits, "in one re- spect they are similar, for both alike are indus- trial organisations concerned ultimately with the same fundamental purpose, the maintenance of the standard of life.' '4 •But he shows that in many respects the two systems are very dis- similar indeed. The Craft Guilds had a re- stricted membership, comprising only skilled artisans; they were local, not national, a guild consisting of the men of a pcirticular locality; membership of the guild Was compulsory. But the vital difference ,Mr. Lipson shows to be the fact that the Craft Guilds did not consist of workmen only, but of all grades of producers, the manual worker, the middle man, and the entrepreneur. There is a greater resemblance between the journeymen guilds and trade unions, but even here the difference is very great. The journeymen were unable to estab- lish a stable and permanent organisation, and as it was always possible for an enterprising journeyman to become a master, such an or- ganisation was out of the- question. Mr. Lipson furnishes us with some interesting information on the economic position of women during this.period, showing that they played a not altogether insignificant part in industry. It is interesting to note that Stress of competi- tion gave rise to an agitation against the em- ployment of women workers, and it is in the silk weaving industry that women' appear to have been mostly employed. . When Venice Rivalled London. .

In a long and interesting chapter-On "Foreign Trade," Mr. LiPson gives us an account of the development of, our overseas eomperce and our relations -with other countries, and one inci- dent in this connection is worth quoting, "The great rival of English traders in the South was Venice, whose supremacy ,in the Mediterranean answered to the Hanseatic • doniinatiOn in the Baltic. div.head: WOULD SACRIFICE HIS LIFE BEFORE
div.p: WOULD SACRIFICE HIS LIFE BEFORE
HIS JOB.

The first appellant was Joseph Davenport, of Park-view, Penketh, who is a general clerk in a tanner's office. He said he made this appeal owing to the fact that the local Tribunal agreed that he had a conscientious objection to war- fare, because they offered to recommend him for some non-combatant service. But to this he greatly objected, as It was connected with the military machine, as well as any of the fighting forces. He objected because it would be cowardice to stand by and let others do the fighting. The idea of the military was not to save life, and if he joined the R A.M.C. he would have to do his best to get a soldier well enough to return to the Front to kill as many as he could. It was stated that the local Tribunal had exempted him from combatant service, but the appellant objected to doing any service at all. His contention was that a man all through life decided the right and wrong of a question, and when he came before the final Tribunal, after this life, the question would be as to whether or not he had done right, regardless of the fact that there was a Military Service Act or not. All war was wrong, and he was- going to have nothing to do with it. Asked in turn as to whether he had a father, mother, sister, or brother, he replied in the negative, adding: "I am alone." The Lord Mayor: Do you belong to any place of gorship?---No but I have attended Sankey Parish Church. The Vicar's Daughter.
Prior to the war, what did you do to prove your conscientious objections to war?—l have declared my views in the Sankey Sunday School, before Penketh Wesleyans, and at the Adult Schools.

Who asked you to go to Sankey Schools?— The Vicar's daughter. I gave an address be- fore the Men's Bible Class. Is the Vicar of Sankey the same man who was in charge then?—Yes. Man Who Is Prepared To Watch England Crushed.

TRIBUNAL.

A tall and muscular farmer, declaring him- self to be a Christadelphian, sought to per- suade the Warrington Rural District Tribunal, on Wednesday afternoon, to grant him total exemption from military service, but they even declined to recommend him for non-combatant service. He asked them to state in Writing their reasons for refusal, but they objected, and handed, him an appeal form. In reply to a question, he said he was' prepared to see England crushed rather than desert his eon-

victions. - The applicant was Percy Bamford (19), of Woodside Farm, Rixton, a cowman and gen- eral farm-hand. He explained that his parents and grand-parents on both sides were Christa- delphians, and he had been reared in the faith. His sect had always had an objection to war, ;ind in the American Civil War that attitude vas respected by their being exempted from service. When Conscription was intro- duced into New Zealand they were also ex- empted. Whatever the consequence he was prepared to stand by his convictions. Bamford proceeded to quote Lord Lansdowne, who had declared that men of deep conscien- tious convictions should be exempted, when Mr. W. Furness, the military representative, intervened with: "That is not in the Act. You can quote statements made by Ministers, but if they are .not embodied in the Act they do not justify your application. What dif- ference is there between the Friends and your denomination?"

div.head: Separate From The World.
div.p: Separate From The World.

Applicant: We have no connection whatever. I do not know anything about the Friends. We have always had these views about mili- tary service. We differ from all other bodies. The Chairman (Mr. George Mather): You do eat and drink, I suppose? Applicant: Yes. (Laughter.) We do not make any use of Law Courts, and marriages are restricted to those of like faith.
